text: More than 3,600 years ago, people built a walled city at Sanxingdui, in Sichuan in south-west China.
Wide canals ran around its thick walls, for watering fields, for boats and for defence.
src: c. 1600 BCE: A walled city is founded at Sanxingdui on the banks of the Yazi River / a Bronze Age culture of Sichuan in south-west China
Canals 20–25 metres wide and 2–3 metres deep surrounded the walls and served for irrigation, inland navigation, defence and flood control

text: Its workers cast big bronze masks and heads with bulging eyes and large ears.
They also made the world's oldest life-sized standing statue of a person, and a bronze tree almost 4 metres high.
src: dozens of large bronze masks and heads with angular human features, exaggerated almond-shaped eyes, some with protruding pupils, and large upper ears
the world’s oldest life-sized standing human statue / a bronze tree almost 4 m high

text: Much later, books told of a kingdom called Shu, whose first ruler, Cancong, had eyes that stuck out.
Many Chinese archaeologists think Sanxingdui belonged to this early kingdom of Shu.
src: The Chronicles of Huayang, compiled under the Jin dynasty (266–420 CE), name its legendary rulers: Cancong, the founder, described as having protruding eyes
Many Chinese archaeologists identify it with the early kingdom of Shu

text: More than 3,000 years ago, gold, bronze and jade objects were broken, burned and carefully buried in pits.
New pits dug between 2020 and 2022 held a gold mask, ivory and traces of silk.
src: 12th–11th centuries BCE: The date radiocarbon dating gives the gold, bronze, jade and pottery objects later found in the sacrificial pits / The objects of the Sanxingdui pits had been broken, perhaps ritually disfigured, then burned and carefully buried
Six new sacrificial pits found between 2020 and 2022 have added hundreds of objects, among them a gold mask, ivory and traces of silk

text: No one knows how the culture ended, but the Shu capital may have moved to Jinsha, 40 km away.
Today its treasures are shown in the Sanxingdui Museum, near where they were found.
src: How the Sanxingdui culture ended is not known / Similar discoveries were made at Jinsha, 40 km away, which has links to the Sanxingdui culture and is thought to have been the relocated capital of the kingdom of Shu
In 1997 the Sanxingdui Museum opened near the original site, close to the city of Guanghan, as the central store and exhibition hall for all Sanxingdui artefacts
